clinicalPearls: GJB2 variants are the single commonest cause of hereditary non-syndromic sensorineural hearing loss, most often inherited as autosomal recessive (locus DFNB1).
The gene encodes connexin 26, a gap-junction protein in cochlear supporting cells and the stria vascularis that is essential for recycling potassium ions within the endolymph.
Hearing loss is usually congenital and prelingual, bilateral, symmetrical and sensorineural, ranging from mild to profound, and may be stable or slowly progressive.
Founder variants differ by population, with a common frameshift (c.35delG) predominating in those of European ancestry and distinct variants in East Asian, Ashkenazi Jewish and other groups.
Combined GJB2 and GJB6 (connexin 30) testing matters, because large GJB6 deletions can cause disease in trans with a single GJB2 variant.
Certain dominant GJB2 variants produce syndromic disease with palmoplantar keratoderma and other skin findings, such as the keratitis-ichthyosis-deafness phenotype.
Vestibular function and inner-ear imaging are typically normal and the auditory nerve is intact, so cochlear implantation yields excellent outcomes.
Early identification through newborn hearing screening followed by prompt habilitation is critical for speech and language development.
reference.pathophysiology: Connexin 26 is a gap-junction protein encoded by GJB2; six connexin subunits assemble into a connexon, and two apposed connexons from neighbouring cells form an intercellular channel. In the cochlea these channels create a syncytial network linking the supporting cells of the organ of Corti with the fibrocytes and cells of the stria vascularis, allowing potassium ions that enter hair cells during mechanotransduction to be recycled back to the endolymph and helping to maintain the endocochlear potential. Loss-of-function biallelic variants disrupt channel assembly or gating, impairing potassium homeostasis and the ionic environment required for hair-cell function, producing sensorineural hearing loss without structural malformation. Because connexin 26 and connexin 30 (GJB6) co-assemble within the same network and their genes lie close together on the same chromosomal region, deletions removing GJB6 or shared regulatory elements can unmask a single GJB2 variant. Certain dominant-negative or gain-of-function variants additionally disturb connexin function in the epidermis, giving the associated keratoderma syndromes and accounting for the phenotypic breadth of GJB2 disease.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital cytomegalovirus infection, the commonest non-genetic congenital hearing loss
Syndromic sensorineural hearing loss (Pendred, Usher, Waardenburg, Jervell-Lange-Nielsen, branchio-oto-renal)
Enlarged vestibular aqueduct and other inner-ear malformations
Mitochondrial hearing loss including aminoglycoside-related susceptibility
Other non-syndromic deafness loci (e.g. STRC, SLC26A4, TMC1)
Acquired perinatal causes such as hypoxia, hyperbilirubinaemia and prematurity
additionalInvestigations: Newborn hearing screening with otoacoustic emissions and automated auditory brainstem response
Age-appropriate audiometry and tympanometry to characterise threshold and configuration
Molecular testing of GJB2 with GJB6 deletion analysis
Broader genetic panel or exome sequencing if GJB2 testing is negative
Congenital cytomegalovirus testing, ideally within the neonatal window
Ophthalmology review and electrocardiography where syndromic causes are considered
Temporal bone imaging (MRI or CT) prior to cochlear implantation
redFlags: Any failed newborn hearing screen requiring prompt diagnostic audiology
Features suggesting a syndrome, such as goitre, pigmentary or skin changes, visual loss, or renal or cardiac anomalies
Progressive, fluctuating or markedly asymmetrical loss prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
Delayed speech and language milestones indicating inadequate early habilitation
reference.prognosis: With early diagnosis and habilitation the outlook is very good, and because the auditory nerve is preserved, hearing aids and cochlear implantation typically yield excellent speech and language outcomes. Recessive GJB2 disease is generally non-syndromic with normal life expectancy.
pitfalls: Assuming all congenital sensorineural hearing loss is GJB2-related and omitting congenital cytomegalovirus and syndromic evaluation
Testing GJB2 alone and missing a GJB6 deletion in trans
Overlooking dominant GJB2 syndromes with skin involvement
Delaying habilitation while awaiting genetic results
Misattributing progressive or asymmetrical loss to GJB2 without re-evaluation
management: There is no disease-specific drug therapy; management centres on early auditory habilitation with hearing aids fitted to the threshold and configuration
Cochlear implantation for severe-to-profound loss, which yields excellent speech outcomes because the auditory nerve is preserved
Early speech and language therapy and communication support, with family choice of listening-and-spoken-language or signing approaches
Serial audiometry to detect progression and adjust amplification, alongside educational and psychosocial support
Coordinate care through an audiovestibular and ENT multidisciplinary team with paediatric and educational input
Offer genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive DFNB1 condition, including combined GJB2 and GJB6 testing and screening of relatives
Assess for syndromic features in dominant variants, with ophthalmology and dermatology review where a keratitis-ichthyosis-deafness phenotype is suspected
